articles.title: Zimbabwe's tobacco anchor in Britain holds at £129m
articles.description: Of every £100 of goods Zimbabwe sells to Britain, £96 is tobacco or beverages. While the wider UK–Zimbabwe trade relationship softened in the year to December 2025, Zimbabwean tobacco held its grip, and the IMF projects Zimbabwean GDP growth of 7.5% in 2025 and 5.0% in 2026. The product that built Zimbabwe's name as an exporter is still doing the work.

more.title: The Apple of haircare gets its German cheque
more.description: Ruka, the London-based textured-hair company founded by Zimbabwean entrepreneur Varaidzo Tendai Moyo and her co-founder Ugorji Agbai, has closed a $4.5m round co-led by Henkel Ventures and Freedom Trail Capital. The deal, which takes lifetime funding to roughly $10m and brings one of the world's largest consumer-goods groups onto the cap table, is the most meaningful endorsement yet of a Zimbabwean diaspora-founded brand.

more.title: Pardon Mapondera: gone but not forgotten at Venice
more.description: The fifth and final piece in our series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Pardon Mapondera, the artist whose practice the room finally arranges itself around, treats discarded plastic and glass jars not as ecological signal but as ritual matter, and produces, in the process, the most quietly devotional installation in the Biennale this year.

more.title: Gideon Gomo: from stone to bronze, the ancestral algorithm at Venice
more.description: The fourth in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Gideon Gomo's first sustained body of bronze work, paired with discarded vehicle number plates and Zimbabwean springstone, is the move of a sculptor at full maturity rethinking the material vocabulary of his country's most internationally legible art form.

more.title: Shumba Maasai in Venice
more.description: At the 61st Biennale, the Zimbabwean artist's day-long procession through the city's campi, performed under the borrowed authority of a Murehwa chief, restages the social-sculpture lineage of Joseph Beuys for a contemporary African discursive practice.

more.title: Franklyn Dzingai: family albums and the neural commons at Venice
more.description: The third in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Franklyn Dzingai's reductive cardboard prints, built from the family album, the magazine clipping, the back-room studio photographs of mid-century Zimbabwe, turn out, on close looking, to be the most precisely engineered work in the room.

more.title: Felix Shumba: charcoal and the practice of disappearance at Venice
more.description: The second in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Felix Shumba's six-metre charcoal wall and his Telephone Reader series anchor a body of work that argues drawing is not the act of capturing the seen, but the act of staying present to what is on its way out of sight.

more.title: UK services share in Zimbabwe rises to 8.2%
more.description: The headline UK services trade with Zimbabwe softened year on year. The structural number underneath it tells the better story: Britain's share of all services Zimbabwe imports rose 2.4 percentage points to 8.2%, the highest measured level in years. As Zimbabwean buyers re-rate their global supplier mix, the UK is taking a bigger slice of the country's services demand.

more.title: Zimbabwe's demand lifts British exports by 14.6%
more.description: The Zimbabwean economy is in its strongest stretch in years: 7.5% GDP growth in 2025, a projected 5% in 2026, and that growth is pulling demand for cars, commercial vehicles, medicines and industrial machinery in with it. UK goods exports to Zimbabwe rose 14.6% on the year, the strongest line in an otherwise soft bilateral picture for Britain.

more.title: NODE earns continental recognition for community empowerment drive
more.description: Gibson Mhaka gibson.mhaka@bmetro.co.zw THE National Organisation for Development and Empowerment (NODE), a Zanu-PF affiliate, has received continental recognition after being honoured at the prestigious iChange Nations Africa Awards held recently in Victoria Falls for its contribution to community empowerment and socio-economic transformation. The recognition places the organisation among a select group of African institutions acknowledged for advancing community development, ethical leadership and initiatives that improve the livelihoods of ordinary citizens. The accolade comes as Zimbabwe accelerates efforts towards attaining Vision 2030, with organisations such as NODE complementing Government programmes aimed at empowering communities in line with President Mnangagwa's development philosophy of leaving no one and no place behind. The awards ceremony brought together former Heads of State, diplomats, traditional leaders, Government officials, development practitioners and civil society representatives from across the continent to celebrate institutions and individuals making a positive impact in their respective countries. Receiving the award on behalf of the organisation, NODE Bulawayo provincial chairman Mr Eddie Benson Muchenje described the honour as a significant endorsement of the organisation's commitment to improving the welfare of vulnerable communities through empowerment and sustainable development initiatives. To NODE, this award is an assurance that the Vision 2030 mantra is achievable through the philosophy of leaving no one and no place behind. We sincerely appreciate the guidance of our mentor, His Excellency President Mnangagwa, whose vision continues to inspire us to serve communities through empowerment and development, he said. Mr Muchenje said the recognition would motivate the organisation to expand programmes that promote patriotism, self-reliance and economic empowerment, particularly among young people. Every citizen has a responsibility to cultivate patriotism and love for Zimbabwe, especially among the youth, who remain the country's future leaders. We believe empowering young people economically and socially is one of the most effective ways of building a prosperous nation, he said. Founded in 2012, NODE has grown into a nationwide empowerment organisation with a presence across Zimbabwe as well as in neighbouring South Africa and Botswana. Its programmes target women, youths, people living with disabilities and other vulnerable groups through initiatives designed to enhance livelihoods, promote entrepreneurship and encourage sustainable community development. Mr Muchenje said the organisation was established to complement national development efforts by addressing socio-economic challenges confronting communities. NODE was founded in 2012 out of a desire to uplift communities by responding to the challenges affecting ordinary Zimbabweans while supporting His Excellency President Mnangagwa's vision of inclusive national development, he said. He said his involvement with NODE evolved from supporting its programmes to assuming leadership of the Bulawayo province after appreciating the impact the organisation was making in communities. I was first drawn to NODE because of its commitment to community service and patriotism. As I became more involved, I realised that its programmes were helping transform lives while complementing the national development agenda. When I was entrusted with leading the Bulawayo province, I accepted the responsibility with humility and determination, he said. Beyond humanitarian assistance, Mr Muchenje said the organisation had shifted its focus towards sustainable empowerment by equipping beneficiaries with practical skills capable of generating long-term income. He said instead of creating dependency through donations alone, NODE was empowering communities through vocational skills, entrepreneurship and income-generating projects. We want people to become economically independent. Through skills development in sectors such as agriculture, mining, fabrication and steelwork, beneficiaries are equipped to earn sustainable incomes, support their families and contribute meaningfully to the country's economic growth, he said. Mr Muchenje said the organisation was also broadening its developmental footprint by pursuing projects capable of transforming communities and creating opportunities for young people. Our vision extends beyond welfare programmes. We are engaging partners on projects that promote infrastructure development, youth empowerment and affordable housing, particularly for self-employed entrepreneurs and small business owners who often struggle to access decent accommodation, he said. He added that NODE had intensified its anti-drug and substance abuse campaigns through its Identify-Rehabilitate-Empower model, which seeks to rehabilitate affected youths before integrating them into productive economic activities. The organisation has also undertaken several community-based social responsibility programmes, including providing assistance to vulnerable groups. Last December, it brought festive cheer to 143 inmates at Anju Farm Prison in Matabeleland North through a Christmas outreach initiative that underscored its commitment to ensuring that no segment of society is left behind. The iChange Nations Africa Awards form part of a global movement that recognises institutions and individuals whose work advances humanity through ethical leadership, community development, humanitarian service and public service. This year's recipients included Deputy Minister of Tourism and Hospitality Industry Tongai Mnangagwa, Minister of State for Matabeleland North Provincial Affairs and Devolution Richard Moyo, Senator Chief Fortune Charumbira, former Mauritian President Professor Ameenah Gurib-Fakim, former African Union Commission chairperson Dr Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma and Nelson Mandela Foundation chief executive officer Dr Sello Hatang, among other distinguished African leaders. For NODE, the continental recognition not only celebrates achievements recorded over the past decade but also affirms the growing role of community-based organisations in complementing Government efforts to build an empowered, inclusive and prosperous Zimbabwe.

more.title: 2026 Chibuku Neshamwari Traditional Dance Festival roars to life
more.description: Mthabisi Tshuma in Harare THE 2026 Chibuku Neshamwari Traditional Dance Festival has burst into life at Harare Gardens, with 10 of Zimbabwe's finest traditional dance ensembles competing for the coveted national title and a US$15 000 grand prize. The annual festival, organised by Delta Corporation through its flagship Chibuku brand in partnership with the National Arts Council of Zimbabwe (NACZ) and the Zimbabwe National Traditional Dance Association (ZNTDA), has drawn performers and cultural enthusiasts from across the country's 10 provinces. [caption id=attachment_5428778 align=aligncenter width=300] 2026 Chibuku Neshamwari Traditional Dance Festival[/caption] The winning group will walk away with US$15 000, while the first and second runners-up will receive US$10 000 and US$7 500 respectively. Representing Matabeleland South is Bolamba Culture Birds, while Bulawayo is represented by Ezimnyama Dance Ensemble. Matabeleland North has fielded Amakhosikazi Dance Ensemble. Other contestants are Shingai Dance Group (Harare), Dapuraunanzva Arts Ensemble (Manicaland), Marondera Gure Club (Mashonaland East), Pisa Pisa Nyau Club (Mashonaland West), Dzimbahwe Nengoma Dance Ensemble (Mashonaland Central), Chipolopolo Nyau Dance Group (Midlands) and Mutimurefu School of Arts (MUSA) from Masvingo. [caption id=attachment_5428773 align=aligncenter width=300] 2026 Chibuku Neshamwari Traditional Dance Festival[/caption] Beyond the energetic performances on stage, Harare Gardens has been transformed into a vibrant celebration of Zimbabwean culture, with festival-goers taking part in traditional games that have added to the festive atmosphere. Attendees have been reliving childhood memories through indigenous games such as tsoro and pads, creating a family-friendly environment that celebrates the country's rich cultural heritage. [caption id=attachment_5428783 align=aligncenter width=300] 2026 Chibuku Neshamwari Traditional Dance Festival[/caption] The festival is expected to conclude with a star-studded after-party headlined by Jah Prayzah, supported by Baba Harare, Nisha Ts and Chillspot Records duo DJ Fantan and Levels. The Chibuku Neshamwari Traditional Dance Festival remains one of Zimbabwe's premier cultural events, providing a platform for preserving and promoting the country's diverse traditional dances while rewarding artistic excellence.
